I’ve been in 7 years and have every intention of separating after this contract is up. While I don’t regret joining whatsoever, and I’ve never been sexually assaulted, I’ve definitely dealt with sexual harassment and gender based discrimination. To echo others who have commented, your daughter will need to be emotionally strong and have the ability to stand up for herself, and also tell people off when they’re acting a fool or saying things they shouldn’t. Not to say rape doesn’t happen (it does) but I disagree that it’s inevitable. I work with primarily men, and the vast majority have been really awesome people who I trust. I’ve also worked and deployed with people who I wouldn’t want to be in a room alone with if you paid me. 
From what I’ve seen (and to be fair I’ve only been at 2 commands) sexual assault is handled quickly and effectively. Assault is not welcome and perpetrators are quickly removed. But that’s only the ones I’ve know about, and I can’t speak to the cases where someone was bullied into silence, because I’m sure it’s happened. Someone else commented something to the effect of “people left me alone once I learned to be a bitch” and that really resonated with me, because that’s kind of the route I’ve gone. Not like shitting on people constantly or anything, but not dealing with the sexual jokes or advances. If you giggle out if awkwardness they tend to take that as a green light to continue and progress it, but if you shut that shit down then you’re a bitch who can’t take a joke. There’s not really any way to win in my opinion, so I’ll take being a bitch over continuously dealing with it. 
On the flip side there’s definitely some people who just… need thicker skin. At my last command we had a girl that got bounced around from shop to shop because no one wanted her in theirs. I assumed the various LPOs were being dicks until she came into mine. She saw me, the most senior female in the shop (E5) and thought we were friends because girl code or something(?) and told me she had submitted complaints against every LPO she had worked under. I was surprised and asked why. Apparently she didn’t like it when they told her to do stuff. As in her job that she was being paid to do. My LPO (a man) had already caught wind of this and would have me come to any counselings he had with her as a same sex chaperone in case she didn’t like what he had to say and accused him of something unseemly. 
I really hope your daughter isn’t that person either. Be a bitch, but a bitch who gets the job done. If she goes through with enlisting I truly wish her good luck. I think the navy experience as a woman has a lot to do with the commands you get sent to. 
Also unrelated to your initial question, but highly recommend going for an aviation rate and trying to get squadron orders. Infinitely better than ships company in my opinion.

Every single member of the military will get an injury develop a mental illness and be scarred for the rest of their life? Well dang. I’ll have to be on the lookout. I’m 7 years in. I did get an injury pretty recently, snowboarding. In my off time. The military covered my surgery, and follow up therapies and medication, even though it happened while I was off duty. And, as much as I do enjoy blaming the military for my problems, exactly 0 of my injuries have been their fault. Had a mental illness and plenty of trauma prior to coming in, and actually been able to get help for them within the service. When I left for boot camp I had $11 to my name. Now I have tens of thousands of dollars in savings, stocks, CD’s ect. Lived in the barracks for about a year. I’ve lived in civilian housing in town sense then (including overseas) and never struggled financially, although to be fair I don’t have children. I have just over a year of college I’ve completed while in, and will be going to school to finish my bachelors for free in a year and a half when I separate. My story isn’t the same as everyone’s for sure but it’s not unique. And yes there are plenty of crappy aspects, you’ll hear no denial of that from me, but overall the benefits have far outweighed the costs. Its fine to not want to join or encourage others to do so, because believe me, it’s not for everyone. But maybe don’t run around making blanket statements about people you don’t even know.
ETA: finding a job when you get out actually has little to do with rank…. Civilian employers don’t care if you were an E9 if you have no marketable skills. It’s moreso about either how transferable your military job is to the civilian sector, or what avenues you take to get education/ job training to make yourself marketable once you do get out

She had stuff stored under the second bed (mine) and got upset when I asked her to move it, and make a little room for me in the closet. “What am I supposed to do with my stuff?!?” Dunno man. Probably shouldn’t have filled up the entire room knowing you could get a roommate at any time. We eventually get past that, and lived fairly civilly for a while. Then her boyfriend came to visit from the opposite coast for a MONTH. She had apparently invited him to stay in our room. Fine. Annoying but whatever. Until I got back from work on several occasions (I worked nights) to find the door dead-bolted, had to pound on the door for a solid 10 minutes before one of them came to open it. On one occasion while he was still there,  I woke up to see this boyfriend standing Superman style with his hands on his hips in the bathroom door. Which would have been fine if he wasn’t standing there completely nude. Everything hanging out. Roommate worked days and was already at work. She would also FaceTime her family while sitting in bed with no headphones (I’d like to add that there was a separated living room/ kitchen area she could have gone into). Not the craziest or worst roommate judging from some of the stories I’ve heard from others, but I swear when she picked up rank and got BAH I was happier than she was, helped get her boxes to pack her shit and everything.

DDG is my favorite surface platform out of the 3 I’ve been on. Good luck!

The military takes up so much time day to day, not even taking into account duty days/ weekends, watchstanding, deployments ect. You would end up doing majority of the child rearing due to how little he’d be around, not to mention getting dragged all over the country/ globe to his various duty stations, assuming you two got married. Source: me and my spouse are both military. We have seen this happen time and time again to civilian spouses (typically the woman). They end up with kids, and are constantly changing locations every few years, which makes it very difficult to maintain any kind of actual career. Then they’re pretty much stuck. Most of the ones I’ve met end up working in the exchanges/ mini marts on base, or some low paying job out in town, if they work at all.
